questions.question: What does Dense-TS change in the classic Two-Stage network to address narrow-model optimization?

options.A: It replaces the dilated convolutions in the Dilated Dense Block with Two-Stage modules and densely connects them
options.B: It removes all dense connections and uses a wider Transformer encoder
options.C: It replaces the Two-Stage modules with a single dilated convolutional layer
options.D: It predicts phase only and bypasses time-frequency feature extraction

questions.rationale: The architecture is made of densely connected Two-Stage modules instead of the classic dilated block followed by serial TS modules.
questions.evidence_quote: To address these issues, we propose the Dense-TS structure, shown in Fig. 1(b). This structure replaces dilated convolutions in Dilated Dense Block with Two-Stage modules, resulting in a network composed entirely of densely connected Two-Stage modules.

questions.question: How are temporal and frequency dependencies handled within one classic Two-Stage feature extraction module?

options.A: The map is reshaped first to BF×T×C and then BT×F×C before restoring the original shape
options.B: The map is pooled to B×T×F and processed only along frequency
options.C: The map is flattened to BTF×C and processed as an unordered sequence
options.D: The map is split into real and imaginary parts and processed by separate decoders

questions.rationale: The two reshapes let serial modules model temporal and frequency dependencies separately.
questions.evidence_quote: Given a spectral feature map D ∈ RB×T ×F ×C, D is reshaped to DT ∈ RBF ×T ×C for temporal dependencies and then reshaped to DF ∈ RBT ×F ×C for frequency dependencies, with the final output Do reshaped to the input size.

questions.question: Which combination defines the output of a Dense-TS block, beyond concatenating the intermediate layer features?

options.A: It adds the input x to 0.2 times the final dense skip representation
options.B: It averages all skips equally and removes the original input
options.C: It multiplies the deepest feature by 0.2 and applies a sigmoid
options.D: It concatenates the input with only the first TS-MVGB output

questions.rationale: Equation (4) uses a scaled final skip tensor plus the original block input, adding an extra residual route.

questions.question: Which view and signal features are chiefly associated with LKE versus LSG in MVGB?

options.A: LKE supplies a large-receptive-field global view for long-range low-frequency features; LSG models local information and high-frequency detail
options.B: LKE is channel attention for high-frequency detail; LSG is the global long-range branch
options.C: LKE estimates phase directly; LSG reconstructs the clean waveform after ISTFT
options.D: LKE and LSG are both recurrent modules that model only temporal context

questions.rationale: The authors distinguish LKE's global context from LSG's local spatial mask modeling.
questions.evidence_quote:
The large kernel depthwise convo-
lutions provide a large receptive field to capture long-range
low-frequency features, while Simple Gate and HardSwish are
designed with lightweight considerations.
The input x is normalized and then divided into two
branches.
Channel Attention (CA) The first branch is Channel At-
tention (CA) [15], which reallocates weights to each channel,
allowing the module to focus more on important channels
while suppressing less significant ones, resulting in a more
precise feature representation [19].
Learnable-Sigmoid Gate (LSG) The LSG shown in Fig.
2 is responsible for establishing local spatial perspectives,
consists of depth-wise convolution, point-wise convolution,
and Learnable-Sigmoid activation function. This branch is
inspired by the Learnable-Sigmoid activation function used
in MP-SENet [5] for generating masks. Its flexibility makes it
crucial for generating accurate masks. This branch focuses on
modeling local information within the feature map, enhancing
high-frequency details and spatial invariance in the spectrum.

questions.question: What does the paper's Consistency Magnitude Loss compare?

options.A: The clean magnitude spectrum and the magnitude spectrum obtained by applying STFT after ISTFT to the network output
options.B: The noisy and clean complex spectra using a learned PESQ discriminator
options.C: The estimated phase with the target waveform after time-domain filtering
options.D: The discriminator score for clean speech against a constant zero target

questions.rationale: The authors compute a minimum distance in magnitude space after synthesizing and reanalyzing the enhanced speech.
questions.evidence_quote: We directly compute the minimum distance between the magnitude spectrum of the twice-STFTed speech and the clean speech magnitude spectrum, as shown in Fig. 3. This loss LMagConsis.is defined as Consistency Magnitude Loss:

questions.question: Why do the authors avoid making Metric Loss part of the final Dense-TS objective despite PESQ gains in some trials?

options.A: Large metric-loss weighting increases spectral discrepancies and can introduce pseudohallucination that harms perceived quality
options.B: Metric Loss reduces parameter count below the hardware-supported minimum
options.C: Metric Loss is non-differentiable even after use of a discriminator
options.D: Metric Loss improves only phase error while the model predicts phase directly

questions.rationale: The reported P=200 condition produced pseudohallucination and the P=400 condition failed, so the final weight for that term is zero.
questions.evidence_quote: Although the PESQ score increases with P, the distances between amplitude, phase, and the complex spectrum also increase. Moreover, when P is too large (e.g., P = 400), training fails. For instance, as shown in Fig. 5, a pseudohallucination distortion is introduced at P = 200, affecting the perceptual quality. Given these observations, we do not employ LMetric in Dense-TS.

questions.question: Under the VoiceBank+DEMAND setup, which STFT and optimization configuration did the authors use?

options.A: Two-second segments, FFT/window 400, hop 100, batch size 2, AdamW, up to one million steps
options.B: One-second segments, FFT 512, hop 256, batch 16, SGD for 100,000 steps
options.C: Four-second segments, FFT 1024, hop 512, batch 8, Adam for 50,000 steps
options.D: Two-second segments, FFT 256, hop 64, batch 32, RMSProp for one million steps

questions.rationale: The experiment specifies each STFT dimension and training setting explicitly.
questions.evidence_quote: Speech samples were segmented into two-second intervals for the short-time Fourier transform, employing an FFT size of 400, a window length of 400, and a hop length of 100. The training process was conducted with a batch size of 2, using the AdamW optimizer [23], and was carried out for up to 1,000,000 steps.

questions.question: How did the two similarly sized model variants compare over training, and what explanation did the authors offer?

options.A: Classic TS converged faster early, but Dense-TS performed better later, attributed to smoother loss landscape from dense connections
options.B: Dense-TS converged faster throughout because it used six channels instead of four
options.C: Classic TS performed better late because dense connections destabilized the narrow model
options.D: The curves were indistinguishable, which the authors attributed to the optimizer

questions.rationale: The comparison controls approximate parameter count while using 6 channels for classic TS and 4 for Dense-TS.
questions.evidence_quote: Fig. 4 shows the training curves for the 6-channel version of the classic Two-Stage framework and the 4-channel version of the Dense-TS framework (with similar parameter counts), both of which use the MVGB approach we proposed. According to the PESQ curves, while the classic Two-Stage structure converges faster in the early stages, the Dense-TS framework can achieve a better performance in the later stages. This improvement is attributed to the smoother loss landscape provided by the dense connections in the narrower model [11].

questions.question: Which VoiceBank+DEMAND comparison best captures the reported efficiency/performance trade-off against Classic TS?

options.A: Both use 14K parameters; Dense-TSNet scores PESQ 3.05 and uses 356M MACs versus Classic TS at 2.96 and 388M
options.B: Dense-TSNet has 0.92M parameters and 388M MACs, while Classic TS has 14K and 356M
options.C: Dense-TSNet scores 2.60 PESQ with 20.9M parameters, while Classic TS scores 3.05
options.D: The models tie at PESQ 2.96, but Dense-TSNet requires twice the MACs

questions.rationale: The table shows the same parameter count, modestly better Dense-TSNet quality scores, and lower multiply-accumulate operations.

questions.question: What ablation pattern most strongly supports the value of LKE in the reported scores, and what caution does SSNR add?

options.A: Removing LKE gives the lowest ablated PESQ (2.79) and COVL (3.61), but its SSNR (8.62) is higher than the full model's 8.16
options.B: Removing CA gives the worst PESQ and raises SSNR above every other variant
options.C: Removing LSG improves PESQ above 3.05 and lowers all other scores
options.D: Removing consistency loss leaves every metric unchanged, proving it has no effect

questions.rationale: LKE ablation most reduces PESQ/COVL, while SSNR moves in the opposite direction, underscoring metric-specific tradeoffs.
